text: of the mag- gots also appears to stimulate the growth of granulation tissue. The maggots are applied to the surface of the wound and kept in place with dressings for up to 3 days. They are removed with the dressing, and the wound is irrigated with sodium chloride solu- tion; any remaining maggots are removed with forceps. Maggots should not be applied to wounds that have a tendency to bleed easily, or that communicate with a body cavity or any internal organ. Pain has been reported with larval therapy and some patients may require analgesics. ◊ References. 1. Courtenay M, et al. Larva therapy in wound management. J R Soc Med 2000; 93: 72–4. 2.
